title: The Nature of Consciousness in Machines
transcript_text: In today's conversation we explore whether consciousness is computational or fundamentally biological. Sarah Chen joined us from Stanford where she runs the consciousness lab. Before Stanford she spent five years at MIT working alongside Marcus Yamamoto on integrated information theory. She argues that current large language models exhibit none of the architectural features required for phenomenal experience even if their outputs sometimes look human-like. The discussion touched on Giulio Tononi's framework and the hard problem of consciousness. Chen pushed back on Geoffrey Hinton's recent claims that large models might have subjective experience. She also mentioned ongoing collaborations with Anil Seth's group at Sussex.

title: AGI Timelines and Hard Limits
transcript_text: James Rodriguez joins us to discuss AGI timelines. Rodriguez previously worked at OpenAI for four years before joining Anthropic in 2023. He thinks the field is collectively overoptimistic about timelines and gives a 20 percent probability to transformative AI before 2035. He worked closely with Dario Amodei on scaling laws research and credits much of his current thinking to those years. He pushed back against shorter timeline arguments from Leopold Aschenbrenner. He brought up the alignment problem repeatedly and stressed that capability gains are outpacing interpretability.

title: Brain-Computer Interfaces in Practice
transcript_text: Aisha Patel discusses the current state of brain-computer interfaces. She runs a lab at MIT focusing on noninvasive recording techniques. Her doctoral work was at Caltech under David Anderson. She is skeptical of Neuralink's claims about general consumer applications and thinks medical applications remain the only credible near-term use case. The conversation covered her collaborations with Edward Boyden on optogenetics and her concerns about commercial pressure distorting the research agenda.

title: The Economics of Compute
transcript_text: Mark Williamson on the economics of compute at frontier AI labs. He has been at DeepMind since 2019 after a decade at Google Brain. The episode covers TPU vs GPU tradeoffs and why model training costs are about to plateau briefly before resuming exponential growth. He mentioned ongoing collaborations with NVIDIA engineers and his earlier work at Google with Jeff Dean on distributed systems. He thinks frontier model training will exceed one billion dollars per run by 2027.

title: Robotics Without Hype
transcript_text: Hiroshi Tanaka discusses the state of household robotics. Tanaka spent fifteen years at Honda Research before moving to TRI in 2021. He is openly critical of recent humanoid robot demonstrations that he calls staged. He worked extensively with Russ Tedrake at MIT during a sabbatical year and credits that collaboration with reshaping his views on differentiable simulation. The conversation covered manipulation, locomotion, and why kitchen robots remain twenty years away despite confident predictions otherwise.

title: Multimodal Models and Their Limits
transcript_text: Emma Bergstrom on multimodal AI. She is at Google DeepMind since 2022 after completing her PhD at ETH Zurich. Her advisor was Andreas Krause. She works on vision-language alignment and is well known for her work on the CLIPSurvey paper. She mentioned an ongoing collaboration with Yejin Choi at the University of Washington. Bergstrom argued that current multimodal models are still fundamentally text models with vision encoders bolted on rather than truly integrated systems.

title: The Alignment Question Revisited
transcript_text: Thomas Lindqvist returns to the show. He spent eight years at MIRI before going independent in 2022. He worked with Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares on early alignment theory. Lindqvist now consults for several frontier labs and is less pessimistic than his MIRI-era writings suggested. He mentioned recent conversations with Paul Christiano about iterated amplification and acknowledged that empirical alignment work has progressed faster than he expected.

title: Open Source LLMs and Their Future
transcript_text: Yuki Sato discusses the open source LLM ecosystem. Sato has been at Meta since 2021 working on the Llama family of models. Before Meta she was at Hugging Face where she collaborated with Thomas Wolf on the Transformers library. She argues that open weights are essential for safety research and pushed back against arguments from Anthropic researchers that frontier models should be closed. She mentioned recent work with Stanford CRFM on evaluation benchmarks.

title: Why Symbolic AI Refuses to Die
transcript_text: Robert Hayes makes the case for symbolic AI. Hayes has been at Edinburgh since 1995 with brief visiting appointments at Stanford and Carnegie Mellon. The conversation covered his recent paper on neurosymbolic integration co-authored with Henry Kautz. He is critical of pure scaling approaches and argues that interpretability requires explicit symbolic structure. He spent significant time discussing his earlier collaborations with John McCarthy at Stanford during a 2003 sabbatical.

title: Reinforcement Learning's Identity Crisis
transcript_text: Liam O'Sullivan on reinforcement learning. He completed his PhD at Berkeley under Pieter Abbeel and stayed on as faculty. He works on offline RL and recently collaborated with Sergey Levine on a survey paper. O'Sullivan thinks the RL community has lost its identity and that most current work is really supervised learning with extra steps. He praised recent work by John Schulman at OpenAI and Anthropic on RLHF but argued the term reinforcement learning is increasingly misleading.

title: Hardware Constraints on AI Progress
transcript_text: Priya Krishnamurthy on hardware. She has been at NVIDIA since 2015 and previously worked at Intel for seven years. Her doctoral work was at Stanford with Bill Dally who is now her colleague at NVIDIA. The conversation covered Hopper, Blackwell, and the looming memory bandwidth wall. She mentioned that recent collaborations with OpenAI engineers have shaped Blackwell's design priorities.

title: The Politics of AI Governance
transcript_text: Catherine Whitfield discusses AI governance. She has been at FHI since 2019 and was previously at the Centre for the Governance of AI in Oxford. She collaborated extensively with Allan Dafoe before he moved to DeepMind. Whitfield is skeptical of voluntary safety commitments from frontier labs and argues that the EU AI Act has serious enforcement gaps. She mentioned ongoing work with Helen Toner and Miles Brundage on compute governance proposals.

title: The Long Tail of AI Safety
transcript_text: Marcus Yamamoto returns for a second appearance. Yamamoto has been at MIT since 2018 working on interpretability. He collaborated with Sarah Chen in the early 2020s on consciousness research before pivoting to mechanistic interpretability. He recently published with Neel Nanda on attention head analysis. Yamamoto argued that the bottleneck in interpretability research is not techniques but the rate at which new models invalidate prior findings.

title: Embodied Cognition and Robot Learning
transcript_text: Rachel Müller on embodied cognition. Müller has been at Stanford since 2010 and runs the Stanford Robotics Center. She collaborated with Sergey Levine on early imitation learning papers. She is critical of the assumption that internet-scale data alone is sufficient for embodied intelligence. She mentioned her recent visit to Toyota Research Institute and conversations there with Hiroshi Tanaka about manipulation benchmarks.

title: Reflections on a Decade in AI Research
transcript_text: Geoffrey Hinton joins for a reflective conversation. Hinton spent years at Google Brain before resigning in 2023 to speak freely about AI risks. He briefly discussed his time at the University of Toronto and his early collaborations with Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio. He acknowledged that his recent public concerns about AI risk have caused tension with Bengio while bringing him closer in views to researchers at Anthropic. The conversation covered his current thinking on consciousness, which Sarah Chen had pushed back against in an earlier episode.
